claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy is single phase.
The controlled intervention is to add 1–3 at.% Nb and then apply solution treatment followed by aging at 700°C for 10 hours.
This intervention produces nanoscale phase separation.
The intervention produces uniformly dispersed nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates in the matrix.
The Nb-rich nanoscale precipitates obstruct crack propagation.
Dislocations bypass the precipitates through Orowan looping.
The precipitates distribute stress more evenly.
Nb modification under the specified processing conditions increases fracture toughness relative to the Nb-free baseline.
Nb modification under the specified processing conditions improves ductility relative to the Nb-free baseline.
The predicted improvement requires uniformly dispersed precipitates without continuous brittle phases.
The hypothesis is expected to hold only for 1–3 at.% Nb aged at 700°C for 10 hours.
Changes in precipitate size or distribution may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Formation of continuous Nb-rich brittle phases may cause embrittlement rather than toughness improvement.
The proposed experiment compares alloys containing 0, 1, 2, and 3 at.% Nb after identical heat treatment.
TEM, K_IC, and strain-to-failure measurements can test the proposed mediator and outcomes.

contradictions.description: Continuous brittle Nb-rich phases are defined as outside the conditions under which the mechanism should hold, yet their observation is also presented as falsifying the hypothesis. A boundary-condition violation does not by itself falsify the hypothesis restricted to uniformly dispersed precipitates.
